title: Traditional IRA and Roth IRA
answer: Traditional IRA and Roth IRA are individual retirement accounts. Traditional IRA contributions may be deductible depending on income and workplace-plan coverage; qualified Roth IRA distributions can be tax-free. The annual IRA contribution limit is generally shared across Traditional and Roth IRAs, and eligibility depends on tax year, age, compensation and income. Check current IRS limits before quoting a dollar amount.

title: Roth conversions
answer: A Roth conversion moves eligible pre-tax retirement assets into a Roth account. Amounts that were not previously taxed are generally included in taxable income for the conversion year. A conversion is different from an annual IRA contribution; it does not use the annual contribution limit. The pro-rata rule may matter when Traditional, SEP or SIMPLE IRA balances contain both pre-tax and after-tax amounts. Consider a tax professional before taking action.

title: Rollovers and direct transfers
answer: A direct rollover generally moves eligible retirement-plan funds directly between custodians or plans. An indirect rollover involves money distributed to the individual and may be subject to a 60-day deadline and other restrictions. Rollovers from employer plans can also be affected by withholding and plan rules. Transfers between IRAs of the same tax type are distinct from 60-day rollovers. Verify eligibility and the receiving account before moving funds.

title: Required minimum distributions
answer: Required minimum distributions (RMDs) are minimum annual withdrawals from certain retirement accounts. Starting age and calculation can depend on birth year, account type and beneficiary status. Roth IRAs generally have no lifetime RMD requirement for the original owner. An RMD amount itself generally cannot be rolled over. Confirm the current IRS rules and account-specific facts.

title: Inherited IRAs
answer: Inherited IRA distribution rules depend on the original owner's date of death, whether they died before or after their required beginning date, the beneficiary's relationship and classification, and account type. Some beneficiaries are subject to a 10-year depletion rule, potentially alongside annual RMDs. Review the exact facts and IRS guidance rather than assuming one timeline applies to everyone.

title: Wash sale basics
answer: A wash sale can occur when securities are sold at a loss and substantially identical securities are purchased within 30 days before or after the sale. The loss may be deferred for tax purposes, with basis adjustments in many taxable-account situations. Cross-account and spouse activity can complicate outcomes. A broker's 1099-B may not capture every scenario.

title: Mutual fund pricing
answer: Most traditional open-end mutual fund purchase and redemption orders execute at the fund's next calculated net asset value (NAV), not necessarily the last price displayed when the order was entered. Order cutoffs and fund-specific rules apply; ETFs trade differently on exchanges.

title: Account verification and phishing
answer: Never share passwords, one-time passcodes or full account identifiers in a chat. If you receive a suspicious link or request for verification, independently navigate to the financial institution's official website or app and contact its published support channel. Do not rely on callback numbers contained in suspicious messages.

title: FDIC vs SIPC protection
answer: FDIC insurance applies to eligible deposits at insured banks, subject to its rules and limits. SIPC protection concerns missing customer securities and cash if a member broker-dealer fails, subject to eligibility and limits; it does not protect against market losses. Brokerage sweep structures may involve different protection arrangements. Check specific program documents.
